photovoltaics-001.question: When light falls on a pn-junction solar cell, which correctly describes how electrical power can be delivered to an external circuit?
choices: Light heats the junction, and the thermoelectric voltage (Seebeck effect) created by the temperature difference between the p and n sides drives a current proportional to that difference through the external load
A forward voltage is applied with an external supply, and the forward current increased by light is delivered to the load, so without a supply no power can be obtained at all
Electron-hole pairs created by light are separated toward the n and p sides by the built-in field, and under a forward voltage a current opposite to the diode's forward current flows through the load
photovoltaics-001.explanation: When minority carriers generated by light diffuse to the junction, the built-in field of the depletion region sends electrons to the n side and holes to the p side. This is the photocurrent, and with the terminals open, electrons collect on the n side and holes on the p side, producing a forward voltage. With a load connected, the voltage stays in the forward direction while the current flows opposite to the diode's forward current, so the cell operates in the quadrant where the product of current and voltage is negative (power is delivered). No external supply is needed, and the effect is distinct from the thermoelectric effect of a temperature difference. Photodiodes at zero bias use the same photovoltaic effect, but solar cells are designed to deliver power over a large area.

photovoltaics-002.question: Which correctly describes the standard test conditions (STC) used to compare solar-cell performance?
choices: An irradiance of 1000 W/m² with the air mass 1.5 spectrum (about 1.5 times the vertical path through the atmosphere) and a cell temperature of 25 °C
The extraterrestrial spectrum (air mass 0) at the solar constant of about 1360 W/m² and a cell temperature of 0 °C
The air mass 1.5 spectrum at an irradiance of 100 W/m² and an ambient temperature of 25 °C, with the cell temperature left to rise under the sunlight
photovoltaics-002.explanation: Air mass (AM) expresses the path of sunlight through the atmosphere relative to 1 for overhead sun, and is roughly 1/cos θ at a zenith angle θ. AM1.5 corresponds to a zenith angle of about 48°, and as a representative terrestrial condition, the AM1.5G spectrum, which includes scattered light, is set to 1000 W/m² (= 100 mW/cm²) and the cell temperature to 25 °C. The extraterrestrial AM0 spectrum (about 1360 W/m²) is used to evaluate solar cells for satellites. Outdoors the cell temperature rises and efficiency falls, so the temperature is specified for the cell itself rather than the ambient air. 100 W/m² is an order-of-magnitude error.

photovoltaics-003.question: Which correctly describes the quantities used with the current-voltage (I-V) characteristic of a solar cell?
choices: The maximum power is the product of the open-circuit voltage V_oc and the short-circuit current I_sc, and the load resistance is chosen as V_oc/I_sc to obtain this power
The fill factor FF is the maximum power P_max divided by the product of V_oc and I_sc; it expresses how square the I-V curve is and is less than 1
The open-circuit voltage is the voltage at the point of maximum current, and the short-circuit current is the current at the point of maximum voltage; the power is maximum at both points
photovoltaics-003.explanation: Shorting the terminals gives the short-circuit current I_sc at zero voltage, and opening them gives the open-circuit voltage V_oc at zero current. At both points either voltage or current is 0, so the power is 0, and between them lies the maximum power point (V_mp, I_mp) where the product of current and voltage is largest. The fill factor is FF = V_mpI_mp/(V_ocI_sc), the ratio of the area of the maximum-power rectangle drawn inside the I-V curve to that of the rectangle formed by V_oc and I_sc. Because of the exponential diode characteristic it never reaches 1, and good crystalline silicon cells have values around 0.8. V_oc × I_sc cannot actually be extracted, and the conversion efficiency is η = V_ocI_scFF/P_in.

photovoltaics-004.question: For a solar cell that follows the ideal diode equation J = J_sc − J₀[exp(qV/kT) − 1] with a short-circuit current density J_sc = 40 mA/cm² and a saturation current density J₀ = 1.0×10⁻¹² A/cm², which is closest to the open-circuit voltage? (Temperature 300 K, kT/q = 0.0259 V.)
choices: About 0.27 V
About 0.63 V
About 1.1 V
photovoltaics-004.explanation: Setting J = 0 gives V_oc = (kT/q) ln(J_sc/J₀ + 1). J_sc/J₀ = 0.040/1.0×10⁻¹² = 4.0×10¹⁰, whose natural logarithm is about 24.4, so V_oc ≈ 0.0259 × 24.4 ≈ 0.63 V. About 0.27 V wrongly uses the common logarithm (about 10.6), and about 1.1 V corresponds to the bandgap of silicon; the open-circuit voltage is always smaller than the bandgap divided by q. Because V_oc is set by the logarithm of J₀, every tenfold reduction in J₀ through lower recombination raises it by about 60 mV (= 0.0259 × ln10). Keeping J₀ low with surface passivation and high-quality crystals is the key to a high V_oc.

photovoltaics-005.question: A solar cell with an open-circuit voltage of 0.70 V, a short-circuit current density of 40 mA/cm² and a fill factor of 0.80 is measured under standard test conditions (irradiance 100 mW/cm²). Which is closest to the conversion efficiency?
choices: About 28%
About 18%
About 22%
photovoltaics-005.explanation: The maximum power density is V_oc × J_sc × FF = 0.70 V × 40 mA/cm² × 0.80 = 22.4 mW/cm². Dividing by the incident 100 mW/cm² gives a conversion efficiency of 22.4%, about 22%. About 28% forgets the fill factor and treats the product of V_oc and J_sc as extractable power; in reality the power is 0 at the open-circuit and short-circuit points. About 18% applies the fill factor twice. Because efficiency is the product of 3 quantities, raising V_oc (reducing recombination), raising J_sc (reducing reflection and incomplete absorption) and raising FF (reducing series resistance and leakage) are all ways to raise it.

photovoltaics-006.question: Which correctly describes the effects of a solar cell's series resistance R_s and parallel (shunt) resistance R_sh on its I-V characteristic?
choices: A large R_s flattens the curve on the open-circuit-voltage side and a small R_sh makes the current fall with voltage on the short-circuit side; both lower the fill factor
A larger R_s lowers the open-circuit voltage and a larger R_sh lowers the short-circuit current, so both series and parallel resistance should be kept as small as possible
Neither R_s nor R_sh has any effect in the open-circuit state because no current flows, so they do not affect the open-circuit voltage or fill factor and lower only the short-circuit current
photovoltaics-006.explanation: Series resistance is the resistance met by current flowing through the electrodes and semiconductor; the larger the current, the more voltage IR_s it consumes, so the curve flattens from the maximum power point toward the open-circuit side and the fill factor falls. In the open-circuit state the current is 0, so R_s does not affect the open-circuit voltage. Parallel resistance is a leakage path that bypasses the junction; if it is small, a leakage current V/R_sh proportional to voltage flows and the curve tilts on the short-circuit side. Leakage steals generated current, so under weak light with a small photocurrent the open-circuit voltage also drops greatly. A good solar cell has small R_s and large R_sh; saying that smaller R_sh is better is backwards. Leakage current flows through R_sh even in the open-circuit state, so saying that neither affects the open-circuit voltage and fill factor is also wrong.

photovoltaics-007.question: Which is the general change when the temperature of a crystalline silicon solar cell rises? (Illumination conditions are unchanged.)
choices: The thermal energy kT of the carriers increases, so the open-circuit voltage rises in proportion to kT/q, and the short-circuit current also increases, so the efficiency rises with temperature
Only the short-circuit current changes with temperature; the open-circuit voltage and fill factor are set by the bandgap alone and do not depend on it, so efficiency stays nearly constant
The saturation current J₀ rises steeply, so the open-circuit voltage falls (about 2 mV per K); the short-circuit current rises slightly, but overall efficiency falls
photovoltaics-007.explanation: The saturation current rises steeply with temperature, as J₀ ∝ nᵢ² ∝ T³exp(−Eg/kT), and in V_oc ≈ (kT/q) ln(J_sc/J₀) the decrease inside the logarithm outweighs the increase in kT/q, so the open-circuit voltage falls. For crystalline silicon this is about −2 mV per K, and the temperature coefficient of efficiency, in relative terms, is said to be roughly −0.3 to −0.5 %/K (depending on the cell structure). As temperature rises the bandgap narrows slightly and absorption at long wavelengths increases, so the short-circuit current rises a little, but the voltage drop has a much larger effect. The fill factor also falls with temperature. Outdoors the cell runs considerably hotter than the ambient air, so module heat dissipation affects energy yield.

photovoltaics-008.question: Which correctly describes the idea behind the theoretical upper limit on the conversion efficiency of a single-junction solar cell (the Shockley–Queisser limit)?
choices: It assumes that all photons with energy above the bandgap are absorbed and all of their energy is converted to electricity, so the limit approaches 100% as the bandgap is made smaller and more light is absorbed
It assumes 1 electron-hole pair per photon, excess energy lost as heat and only radiative recombination, derived from detailed balance; for AM1.5G it is about 33% near 1.3 eV
The limit is simply the Carnot efficiency of about 95% set by the sun's surface temperature of about 5800 K and the cell temperature of 300 K, independent of bandgap
photovoltaics-008.explanation: Shockley and Queisser derived the single-junction efficiency limit from the detailed balance of light absorption and emission between the solar cell and the sun. The major losses are the transmission of light with energy below the bandgap Eg and the conversion of the excess energy of photons above Eg into heat by carrier thermalization. A smaller Eg absorbs more light but lowers the voltage, while a larger Eg raises the voltage but absorbs less light, so for AM1.5G the maximum of about 33% occurs near 1.3–1.4 eV. Radiative recombination, by which the cell itself emits light, cannot be avoided, so the open-circuit voltage is also smaller than Eg/q. The Carnot efficiency of about 95% is the limit for heat engines, not for single-junction solar cells.

photovoltaics-009.question: A silicon solar cell with a bandgap of 1.12 eV absorbs a photon with a wavelength of 500 nm. Roughly what percentage of the photon energy is lost as heat when the resulting electron and hole relax (thermalize) to the band edges? (E[eV] ≈ 1240/λ[nm].)
choices: About 55%
About 45%
Almost 0% (the excess energy creates a 2nd electron-hole pair)
photovoltaics-009.explanation: The photon energy is 1240/500 ≈ 2.48 eV. Electrons and holes relax to the band edges within a short time of a ps or less by emitting phonons, so the 2.48 − 1.12 = 1.36 eV above Eg becomes heat, a fraction of 1.36/2.48 ≈ 0.55, about 55%. About 45% is the fraction 1.12/2.48 that remains at the band edges, confused with the fraction lost. The process in which 1 photon creates 2 or more pairs occurs only slightly in silicon with ultraviolet light and hardly at all with 500 nm light, so the loss is not almost 0%. Reducing this thermalization loss is the idea behind tandem solar cells, which stack cells with different bandgaps.

photovoltaics-010.question: Which is a property of a solar cell whose open-circuit voltage is close to the theoretical limit?
choices: The less light it emits in the open-circuit state the better, since materials that emit light on recombination lose more of the generated power and so have a lower open-circuit voltage
In the open-circuit state all carriers recombine inside the cell, so the open-circuit voltage is higher the less non-radiative recombination and the higher the external luminescence efficiency
The open-circuit voltage is set by the bandgap alone (about 1.12 V for silicon) and does not depend on the kind of recombination, the luminescence efficiency or non-radiative losses
photovoltaics-010.explanation: In the open-circuit state no current is extracted, so all generated carriers recombine inside the cell. If recombination is purely radiative, the carrier density stays as high as possible and the open-circuit voltage reaches the detailed-balance limit. Non-radiative recombination removes carriers sooner and lowers the open-circuit voltage by (kT/q)|ln ηext|, where ηext is the external luminescence efficiency; at ηext = 1% it is about 0.12 V lower at 300 K. Photon recycling, in which photons from radiative recombination are reabsorbed, also helps, so high-efficiency GaAs cells are designed for light extraction as well. Emitting light is not itself a loss; recombination that turns into heat without emitting light is what lowers the open-circuit voltage. The open-circuit voltage is always below the bandgap divided by q, and the difference is set by recombination.

photovoltaics-011.question: Which correctly describes how the external quantum efficiency (EQE, the number of electrons delivered to the external circuit per incident photon) of a crystalline silicon solar cell varies with wavelength?
choices: At long wavelengths absorption is weak and incomplete, so it falls toward about 1100 nm, and at short wavelengths it falls through losses to surface recombination
EQE is proportional to photon energy, so it rises toward shorter wavelengths and peaks for ultraviolet light absorbed near the surface
EQE is constant at all wavelengths shorter than the bandgap wavelength, does not include the effects of surface reflection or incomplete absorption, and does not depend on cell thickness
photovoltaics-011.explanation: EQE is the ratio of electrons to photons that includes all losses from reflection, incomplete absorption and carrier collection. Silicon is an indirect semiconductor whose absorption coefficient is small at wavelengths near the bandgap, about 1100 nm, so a cell 100-odd µm thick cannot absorb all the light, and light trapping that lengthens the light path with surface texture and rear reflection is effective. Ultraviolet and blue light is absorbed within roughly 0.5 µm of the surface, so it is more exposed to losses from surface recombination and heavily doped layers. The value expressed per absorbed photon, excluding reflection, is the internal quantum efficiency (IQE). Because it is a ratio of photon counts, it does not rise in proportion to photon energy, and it is a different quantity from responsivity per unit power.

photovoltaics-012.question: Of AM1.5G sunlight (1000 W/m²), take the number of photons with energy above the bandgap of silicon (1.12 eV) to be 2.7×10¹⁷ /(cm²·s). Which is closest to the short-circuit current density of a cell whose average external quantum efficiency for these photons is 90%? (q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.)
choices: About 43 mA/cm²
About 3.9 mA/cm²
About 39 mA/cm²
photovoltaics-012.explanation: The short-circuit current density is the number of electrons extracted times the elementary charge: J_sc = qΦ × EQE = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 2.7×10¹⁷ × 0.90 ≈ 3.9×10⁻² A/cm², about 39 mA/cm². About 43 mA/cm² takes the external quantum efficiency as 100%, which corresponds to the upper limit of an ideal cell with no reflection or recombination. About 3.9 mA/cm² is off by one order of magnitude in converting A to mA. In reality the external quantum efficiency varies with wavelength, so J_sc = q∫EQE(λ)Φ(λ)dλ is obtained by multiplying the measured EQE spectrum by the photon numbers of the standard spectrum and summing, which is also used to check the current measured with a solar simulator.

photovoltaics-013.question: Which correctly describes a tandem solar cell in which 2 cells with different bandgaps are stacked from the illuminated side and connected in series with 2 terminals?
choices: The larger-bandgap cell is placed on the illuminated side; the voltage is roughly the sum of both, but the current is limited by the weaker cell, so the currents are matched
The cell with the smaller bandgap is placed on the illuminated side to absorb a wide range of wavelengths first, and the light it transmits is used by the lower cell with the larger bandgap
The currents of the 2 cells add while the voltage equals that of the lower-voltage cell, so the bandgaps are chosen close to each other to match the open-circuit voltages of the 2 cells
photovoltaics-013.explanation: Placing the larger-bandgap cell on top lets high-energy photons be used at a high voltage, reducing thermalization loss. Light transmitted by the top cell is absorbed by the lower, smaller-bandgap cell. If the smaller-bandgap cell were on top, it would absorb almost all the light and none would reach the lower cell. In a 2-terminal series connection the same current flows through both cells, so the voltages add, but the current is set by the weaker cell; for example, if the top cell gives 19 mA/cm² and the bottom 21 mA/cm², only about 19 mA/cm² can be extracted. The thickness or bandgap of the top cell is therefore adjusted to equalize the currents (current matching). A 4-terminal configuration with separate terminals for each cell does not need current matching.

photovoltaics-014.question: Which is correct about solar cells that use metal halide perovskites (for example CH₃NH₃PbI₃ or compositional variants) as the absorber layer?
choices: They are indirect semiconductors with small absorption coefficients, so, like silicon, they need layers 100 µm or more thick to absorb light and cannot be made by coating
Even slight crystal defects stop them from generating power, so, like silicon, they can only be made by growing single crystals at high temperature
The bandgap can be tuned through the halogen composition, suiting them to the top cell of a tandem with silicon, but stability against moisture, heat and light is a challenge
photovoltaics-014.explanation: Halide perovskites are direct-gap materials with large absorption coefficients, so films a few hundred nm thick absorb sunlight well, and the films can be made by solution coating or low-temperature evaporation. Even in polycrystalline films, most defects form shallow levels near the band edges and do little harm (defect tolerance), which together with the long carrier diffusion lengths is considered a reason for their high efficiency. Replacing iodine with bromine widens the bandgap, so in a tandem with silicon (1.12 eV) they can form a top cell of around 1.7 eV. On the other hand, decomposition and ion migration caused by moisture, heat and light lead to degradation, and ion migration also causes hysteresis, in which the I-V curve changes with scan direction and speed, so the output is checked by tracking the maximum power point for some time.

photovoltaics-015.question: A solar cell with an ideality factor of 1 receives light concentrated 100 times by a lens (100 suns). If the short-circuit current is proportional to light intensity and the cell is held at 300 K (kT/q = 0.0259 V), which is closest to the change in open-circuit voltage?
choices: It rises by about 0.05 V
It rises by about 0.12 V
It does not change (only the current becomes 100 times larger)
photovoltaics-015.explanation: Since V_oc ≈ (kT/q) ln(J_sc/J₀), a 100-fold J_sc raises V_oc by (kT/q) ln100 = 0.0259 × 4.61 ≈ 0.12 V. The power grows by the factor of 100 in current plus the rise in voltage, so if series-resistance losses are small, the conversion efficiency rises too. About 0.05 V wrongly uses the common logarithm log₁₀100 = 2. The open-circuit voltage grows with the logarithm of the current, so saying it does not change is also wrong. In practical concentrator systems, series-resistance loss from the large current and cell heating must be kept down, and lenses can collect only direct sunlight arriving from one direction, so a mount that tracks the sun is also needed. High-concentration systems use high-efficiency III-V multijunction cells.

photovoltaics-016.question: In a silicon solar cell with a randomly textured, light-scattering front surface and a reflective rear surface, the path length of weakly absorbed long-wavelength light is extended to several tens of times the thickness. Which is the main reason the scattered light is trapped in the cell? The refractive index of silicon is about 3.5.
choices: Of the light randomized in direction by scattering, only the narrow cone within the critical angle (about 17°) can escape through the surface; the rest is totally reflected back and makes many passes

The texture varies the antireflection coating thickness from place to place so that light in every direction is no longer reflected at the surface, and light reflected from the rear is absorbed instead of escaping
Scattered light shifts to longer wavelengths, where the absorption coefficient of silicon is larger, so it is absorbed before traveling several tens of thicknesses
photovoltaics-016.explanation: In a flat cell, light reflected from the rear returns in the direction it came and simply escapes after a round trip. Scattering the light randomly at the surface spreads it in all directions inside the cell, but only light heading within the cone sinθ < 1/n, a critical angle of about 17° for silicon, can escape, a fraction of roughly 1/n². The rest is totally reflected back inside and makes many passes while being scattered repeatedly. With ideal Lambertian scattering, the path becomes up to 4n² ≈ 49 times the thickness. An antireflection coating cannot eliminate reflection for all directions; the trapping mechanism is in fact total internal reflection at the surface. Scattering does not change the wavelength of the light, nor the absorption coefficient.

photovoltaics-017.question: In a p-type silicon substrate, the minority-carrier electrons have a diffusion coefficient of 30 cm²/s and a lifetime of 100 µs. Which value is closest to the diffusion length L = √(Dτ)?
choices: About 55 µm
About 30 µm
About 550 µm
photovoltaics-017.explanation: Dτ = 30 cm²/s × 100×10⁻⁶ s = 3.0×10⁻³ cm², so L = √(3.0×10⁻³ cm²) ≈ 0.055 cm = 550 µm. The diffusion length indicates how far photogenerated minority carriers travel before recombining; if it is much longer than the cell thickness (a little over 100 µm for crystalline silicon), electrons generated deep in the cell still reach the junction and contribute current. About 55 µm is off by a factor of ten in converting cm to µm, and about 30 µm reads 3.0×10⁻³ as centimeters without taking the square root. The lifetime is shortened by recombination at impurities and defects, and since L is proportional to √τ, reducing the lifetime to 1/100 cuts the diffusion length to 1/10.

photovoltaics-018.question: In a solar module made of many cells connected in series, a single cell becomes shaded. Which combination correctly describes this situation and the role of bypass diodes connected in antiparallel across groups of cells?
choices: The shaded cell merely produces no voltage and has no effect on the other cells; the bypass diode prevents current from flowing back into the module from a battery or the grid at night
The shaded cell is reverse-biased by the voltage of the other cells and dissipates power as heat (a hot spot); the bypass diode routes the current around that group
The photocurrent in the shaded cell increases, causing overcurrent, so the bypass diode drains the excess current and matches the module current to that of the illuminated cells
photovoltaics-018.explanation: Cells in series carry the same current, so one shaded cell with a small photocurrent limits the current of the whole string. When the other cells try to force current through it, the shaded cell is reverse-biased and dissipates power instead of generating it, heating up locally (a hot spot). With a bypass diode across each group of a dozen or two cells, the diode conducts once that group's voltage goes negative, routing the current around it; the reverse bias on the cell is limited and the remaining groups keep generating. Blocking reverse current at night is the job of a series blocking diode. Shading never increases the photocurrent.

photovoltaics-019.question: When a solar array is connected to an inverter, why is maximum power point tracking (MPPT) control used?
choices: The maximum-power voltage changes with irradiance and cell temperature, so the voltage is stepped slightly while watching whether power rises or falls, keeping operation at the maximum power point
The maximum-power voltage equals the open-circuit voltage, so measuring the open-circuit voltage once and fixing the operating point there gives maximum power at any irradiance or temperature
The maximum power point is fixed by the cell material alone and does not change with irradiance or temperature, so keeping the voltage once set prevents degradation of the cells
photovoltaics-019.explanation: The output power P = IV of a solar cell is zero at both short circuit (V = 0) and open circuit (I = 0) and peaks at the maximum power point in between. When the light weakens, the current falls almost proportionally and the voltage drops slightly, logarithmically. When the temperature rises, the open-circuit voltage drops, and so does the maximum-power voltage. Methods such as hill climbing, which perturb the operating voltage slightly and move in the direction of increasing power, therefore keep following the maximum power point as conditions change. At the open-circuit voltage the current and hence the power are zero; for crystalline silicon the maximum-power voltage is about 80% of the open-circuit voltage. Claiming the maximum power point is fixed overlooks its dependence on temperature and irradiance.

photovoltaics-020.question: A heavily doped p⁺ layer (a back surface field, BSF) is formed at the rear of a solar cell on a p-type silicon substrate. Which statement correctly describes its function?
choices: The p⁺ layer absorbs light strongly, so it absorbs long-wavelength light that has passed through the silicon and generates new electron-hole pairs, increasing the current
A second pn junction forms between the p⁺ layer and the substrate, adding its voltage in series with the front junction, so the open-circuit voltage nearly doubles

The field from the p-to-p⁺ doping step pushes minority-carrier electrons back from the rear surface, reducing recombination at the rear contact and raising the open-circuit voltage and the long-wavelength response
photovoltaics-020.explanation: Minority-carrier electrons photogenerated in the substrate are lost by recombination if they reach the rear contact before being collected at the front junction. A heavily doped p⁺ layer at the rear creates an energy step (a field) in the conduction band at the p-p⁺ boundary that pushes electrons back into the substrate. The effective rear surface recombination velocity drops, so the saturation current falls and the open-circuit voltage rises, and the current from long-wavelength light absorbed near the rear also increases. Since p and p⁺ are both p-type, they do not form a pn junction and add no voltage. Recombination is fast in a heavily doped layer, so carriers generated by light absorbed there contribute almost no current.

photovoltaics-021.question: A solar module with a nominal operating cell temperature (NOCT, the cell temperature at 800 W/m² irradiance and 20 °C air) of 45 °C is used outdoors at an air temperature of 30 °C and irradiance of 1000 W/m². Estimating the cell temperature as T_cell = T_air + (NOCT − 20) × G/800 and taking the temperature coefficient of maximum power as −0.40 %/K (referenced to 25 °C), the output is about what percentage of that at the same irradiance and 25 °C?
choices: About 98%
About 92%
About 86%
photovoltaics-021.explanation: The cell temperature is T_cell = 30 + (45 − 20) × 1000/800 = 30 + 31.25 ≈ 61 °C. That is about 36 K above 25 °C, so the output falls by 0.40 %/K × 36.25 K ≈ 14.5%, to about 86%. About 98% takes the 30 °C air temperature as the cell temperature, and about 92% takes the 45 °C NOCT as the cell temperature; both miss that sunlight heats the cell well above the surrounding air. NOCT reflects how easily the module sheds heat, and mounting it flush on a roof with poor ventilation behind it raises the cell temperature further. On clear summer days the output is therefore often below its rating despite strong irradiance.

photovoltaics-022.question: In p-type silicon cells, instead of covering the whole rear with an aluminum alloy layer (Al-BSF), the PERC structure covers the rear with a dielectric film such as Al₂O₃ and connects the metal contact only through small openings in the film. Which is the main reason this raises efficiency?
choices: Current crowds through the small openings in the film, strengthening the field and accelerating carriers so the contacts collect them more easily, which increases the short-circuit current
The dielectric film greatly reduces rear recombination (the negative fixed charge of Al₂O₃ also repels electrons), and the film–metal stack reflects long-wavelength light well
The dielectric film absorbs ultraviolet sunlight, converts it into long-wavelength light that silicon absorbs well, and sends it back into the cell from the rear
photovoltaics-022.explanation: In an Al-BSF cell the whole rear touches the metal and alloy layer, where recombination limits the open-circuit voltage, and the aluminum rear reflects long-wavelength light poorly. PERC passivates most of the rear with a dielectric film, reducing recombination at dangling bonds. Al₂O₃ carries negative fixed charge, which adds field-effect passivation by repelling minority electrons from the p-type surface. The dielectric–metal stack also forms a good rear reflector that returns weakly absorbed long-wavelength light into the cell. This raises the open-circuit voltage and long-wavelength response. Current crowding at the openings actually adds resistance, so the opening spacing is a trade-off with resistance. The structure does not convert UV into longer wavelengths.

photovoltaics-023.question: For the ideality factor n in the dark current–voltage characteristic of a solar cell written as J ∝ exp[qV/(nkT)], which statement is correct?
choices: n ≈ 1 when diffusion current in the neutral regions dominates and approaches 2 when defect-mediated recombination in the depletion region dominates; a larger n tends to lower the fill factor
n expresses the size of the series resistance: doubling the series resistance doubles n, and an ideal cell with no resistance has n = 0
A larger n indicates a better cell with less recombination; an ideal cell has n = 2, and n = 1 indicates many defects
photovoltaics-023.explanation: The ideality factor describes how fast the current rises as the voltage increases and hints at which recombination sets the current. When injected minority carriers diffuse and recombine in the neutral regions (including radiative recombination), n = 1; when recombination through defect levels in the depletion region dominates, both electrons and holes are involved and n ≈ 2. A larger n makes the current rise more gently with voltage, rounding the corner of the I–V curve and lowering the fill factor. n describes the exponential growth of the current and is distinct from series resistance. An ideal cell has n = 1, so the option that reverses good and bad is also wrong.

photovoltaics-024.question: For a solar cell used under white-LED indoor lighting (almost all the light between about 400 and 700 nm, with very little infrared), which combination of the band gap giving the highest efficiency and the reason is correct?
choices: About 1.1 eV: as under sunlight, absorbing out to the longest possible wavelength increases the current, so silicon cells are already the most efficient
About 3.0 eV: a larger band gap raises the voltage, so the efficiency keeps rising with voltage even if most visible light is transmitted
About 1.9 eV: there is little light beyond the absorption edge (about 650 nm), so widening the gap loses little light and raises the voltage
photovoltaics-024.explanation: In the Shockley–Queisser picture, the optimum band gap balances the transmission of photons below the gap against the thermalization of photons above it. White-LED light is concentrated in the visible, with almost nothing beyond about 700 nm (about 1.8 eV), so widening the gap to around 1.9 eV loses little light and raises the voltage, and the efficiency limit is higher than under sunlight. Silicon at 1.1 eV chooses a low gap for infrared that never arrives, so thermalization losses are large. At 3.0 eV most visible light cannot be absorbed, and the current drops sharply. Wide-band-gap materials are being studied as small power sources for indoor use.

photovoltaics-025.question: A solar cell has a current density J_mp = 38 mA/cm² and voltage V_mp = 0.60 V at the maximum power point. Which combination is closest for the voltage drop J_mp R_s due to an area-specific series resistance R_s = 1.0 Ω·cm², and the power lost in the resistance, J_mp²R_s, as a fraction of the maximum power J_mp V_mp?
choices: Voltage drop 3.8 mV, power loss about 0.63%
Voltage drop 38 mV, power loss about 6.3%
Voltage drop 38 mV, power loss about 1.4%
photovoltaics-025.explanation: The voltage drop is J_mp R_s = 0.038 A/cm² × 1.0 Ω·cm² = 0.038 V = 38 mV. The lost power is J_mp²R_s = 0.038² × 1.0 ≈ 1.44 mW/cm², and the maximum power is 38 mA/cm² × 0.60 V = 22.8 mW/cm², so the fraction is 1.44/22.8 ≈ 6.3% (= 38 mV/0.60 V). About 1.4% expresses the loss as a fraction of the 100 mW/cm² incident light, not of the maximum power. 3.8 mV and about 0.63% come from a slip in converting mA to A. Series-resistance loss grows with the square of the current, so grid-finger design and resistance reduction matter most for high-current cells and concentrator cells.

photovoltaics-026.question: For a solar cell with ideality factor 1 and no series- or shunt-resistance effects, the fill factor is well approximated by the empirical formula FF ≈ [v_oc − ln(v_oc + 0.72)]/(v_oc + 1), where v_oc = V_oc/(kT/q). Which value is closest to FF for V_oc = 0.70 V and kT/q = 0.0259 V?
choices: About 0.96
About 0.85
About 0.21
photovoltaics-026.explanation: v_oc = 0.70/0.0259 ≈ 27.0, so FF ≈ (27.0 − ln27.7)/(27.0 + 1) = (27.0 − 3.32)/28.0 ≈ 0.846, about 0.85. About 0.96 drops the logarithmic term in the numerator and gives v_oc/(v_oc + 1), ignoring that the maximum-power voltage lies well below V_oc. About 0.21 uses 0.70 directly as v_oc without dividing V_oc by the thermal voltage. The larger v_oc, the squarer the I-V curve and the larger FF, so cells with higher V_oc also have higher FF. In real cells, series and shunt resistance and an ideality factor above 1 make FF smaller than this value.

photovoltaics-027.question: Seen from the ground, the solar disk has an apparent angular radius of about 0.267°. When sunlight is concentrated in air, the upper limit on concentration set by conservation of étendue is C_max = 1/sin²θ, where θ is the Sun's apparent radius. Which value is closest to this limit?
choices: About 4.6×10⁴ times
About 1.2×10⁴ times
About 2.1×10² times
photovoltaics-027.explanation: θ = 0.267° = 4.66×10⁻³ rad, so sinθ ≈ 4.66×10⁻³ and sin²θ ≈ 2.17×10⁻⁵, giving C_max = 1/sin²θ ≈ 4.6×10⁴ times. About 1.2×10⁴ times uses the apparent diameter 0.533° in place of the radius. About 2.1×10² times is 1/sinθ, the limit for a linear concentrator that concentrates in one direction only (such as a trough). The closer the concentration comes to the limit, the narrower the range of incidence angles the concentrator can accept, down to about the size of the Sun, so it must track the Sun precisely. Inside a medium of index n the concentration can be a further n² times higher. Practical concentrator cells operate at a few hundred to about a thousand times.

photovoltaics-028.question: Solar cells made from boron-doped p-type Czochralski (CZ) silicon can lose a few percent (relative) of their efficiency within hours to days of first exposure to light (light-induced degradation, LID). Which combination of cause and remedy is correct?
choices: Ultraviolet light yellows the antireflection coating and lowers its transmittance, so switching to a UV-resistant coating material eliminates the degradation
Light heats the cell and widens the silicon band gap, and the efficiency recovers as soon as the cell cools, so no countermeasure is needed
Under light-injected carriers, boron and oxygen in the crystal form complexes that act as recombination centers and cut the lifetime; doping with gallium instead suppresses it
photovoltaics-028.explanation: CZ crystals contain oxygen dissolved from the quartz crucible. When light injects carriers, boron–oxygen complexes (B-O defects) form and reduce the minority-carrier lifetime, lowering the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current. Remedies include replacing boron with gallium as the p-type dopant, using crystals with less oxygen, and treatments that illuminate the cell while heating it to deactivate the defects (regeneration). Raising the temperature actually narrows the band gap, and a temperature effect that recovers on cooling is a separate matter from LID. Discoloration of the antireflection coating is not the cause either; LID takes place in the crystal of the cell.

photovoltaics-029.question: Organic thin-film solar cells use as the absorber a blended layer (bulk heterojunction) in which an electron-donating material (donor) and an electron-accepting material (acceptor) are intermixed on a scale of a few tens of nanometers or less. Which statement correctly gives the reason?
choices: Light creates tightly bound excitons that move only about 10 nm before decaying, so a nearby donor–acceptor interface splits them into electrons and holes
Organic materials have small absorption coefficients, so the two materials are mixed to make the layer micrometers thick and lengthen the light path to increase absorption
In organic materials light creates free electrons and holes directly, so the two materials are mixed only to add conduction paths and lower the series resistance
photovoltaics-029.explanation: Organic semiconductors have a low dielectric constant, so the electron and hole created by light form an exciton tightly bound by the Coulomb force, which room-temperature thermal energy cannot split. An exciton diffuses only about 10 nm during its lifetime, so if a donor–acceptor interface lies within that range, the energy offset transfers the electron to the acceptor and the hole to the donor, separating them. Intermixing the two materials on a scale of tens of nanometers or less means an exciton formed anywhere in the film can reach an interface, and the separated electrons and holes travel through their own materials to the electrodes. Organic materials absorb strongly, so a film about 100 nm thick is enough. Light creates free carriers directly in inorganic semiconductors such as silicon.

photovoltaics-030.question: Thin metal electrodes (fingers) are laid out at regular intervals on the front of a crystalline silicon solar cell. Which statement correctly explains how the finger spacing is chosen?
choices: More electrodes collect current more easily with no loss, so covering the whole surface with metal would be ideal, and the spacing is widened only to save material cost
Narrow spacing shades more area and wide spacing raises the lateral resistive loss in the surface layer, so the spacing that minimizes the total is chosen
The spacing is made an integer multiple of the light wavelength so that light diffracted by the electrodes travels along the surface, strengthening light trapping in the cell
photovoltaics-030.explanation: Carriers generated by light flow sideways through the thin emitter layer at the surface to reach the fingers. Widening the finger spacing lengthens this lateral path, increasing the resistive loss and lowering the fill factor. Narrowing it reduces the resistive loss, but metal electrodes block light, so the shaded area grows and the short-circuit current falls. The spacing that minimizes the sum of the two losses is therefore chosen according to the emitter sheet resistance and the finger width. Covering the whole surface with metal would let no light in and produce no power. The spacing is on the millimeter scale, far larger than the wavelength, and has no light-trapping role through diffraction. Printing the fingers narrow and tall reduces both shading and resistance.

photovoltaics-031.question: A single-layer antireflection coating of silicon nitride (SiNₓ) with refractive index 2.0 is applied to a crystalline-silicon solar cell. For minimum reflection at 600 nm, which value is closest to the film thickness? (Assume normal incidence and an optical thickness of λ/4.)
choices: About 150 nm
About 300 nm
About 75 nm
photovoltaics-031.explanation: An optical thickness nd of λ/4 gives d = λ/(4n) = 600/(4 × 2.0) = 75 nm. Light reflected from the top and bottom of the film then differs by half a wavelength after the round trip and cancels. About 150 nm is λ/4 without dividing by the index, or λ/(2n); a film whose optical thickness is half a wavelength reflects as if it were absent. About 300 nm is λ/2 and does not reduce reflection either. The film index that brings reflection to nearly zero is the square root of the product of the indices of air and silicon (about 3.9), about 2.0; SiNₓ is close to this and also passivates the surface against recombination, so it is widely used. Cells look deep blue because the reflection minimum lies near 600 nm and some shorter-wavelength light is reflected.

photovoltaics-032.question: A solar cell has an external quantum efficiency of 90% at 800 nm. Which value is closest to its spectral responsivity at this wavelength (short-circuit current per watt of incident optical power)? (E[eV] ≈ 1240/λ[nm])
choices: About 0.65 A/W
About 0.58 A/W
About 1.4 A/W
photovoltaics-032.explanation: Each photon carries 1240/800 = 1.55 eV, so 1 W of light delivers 1/(1.55 × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹) photons per second. If 90% of them yield electrons, the current is 0.90/1.55 ≈ 0.58 A/W. In general the spectral responsivity is SR = EQE × λ[nm]/1240. About 0.65 A/W forgets to multiply by the external quantum efficiency. About 1.4 A/W inverts λ/1240 to 1240/λ; with EQE at most 1, the responsivity at 800 nm cannot exceed 0.65 A/W. At the same EQE the responsivity rises with wavelength, because each photon carries less energy and the same power brings more photons.

photovoltaics-033.question: Heterojunction solar cells, in which a few nanometers of intrinsic amorphous silicon (a-Si:H) and p- and n-type amorphous silicon layers are deposited on both sides of crystalline silicon, readily reach high open-circuit voltages. Which is the main reason?
choices: The a-Si:H passivates surface dangling bonds with hydrogen and keeps the contacts off the crystal, greatly reducing recombination at surfaces and contacts
Amorphous silicon has a smaller band gap than the crystal and absorbs long-wavelength light the crystal cannot, raising both current and voltage
Mobilities in the amorphous layers exceed those of the crystal, so carriers reach the contacts quickly and series-resistance losses vanish
photovoltaics-033.explanation: The open-circuit voltage is set by the logarithm of the recombination-limited saturation current J₀, and in crystalline-silicon cells recombination at the surfaces and where metal contacts touch the crystal is a major loss. In a heterojunction cell, a thin intrinsic a-Si:H layer passivates the crystal surface by terminating dangling bonds with hydrogen, and the doped a-Si:H layers form carrier-selective junctions that keep the contacts separated from the crystal. Recombination under the contacts also drops sharply, J₀ becomes small, and the open-circuit voltage rises to about 0.75 V. Amorphous silicon has a larger band gap than the crystal, about 1.7 eV, so it is not a layer for absorbing long wavelengths. Its mobilities are actually lower, and it does not reduce resistance.

photovoltaics-034.question: Bifacial solar modules also generate power from light reaching their rear side. Which correctly describes how their output depends on installation conditions?
choices: The rear side receives no direct sunlight, so regardless of ground reflectance or mounting height the output is a nearly constant few percent above a monofacial module
Rear-side cells become more efficient as front-side light heats them, so the rear contribution is largest in summer with strong sunshine
The higher the ground reflectance (albedo), and the higher the module is mounted so light can reach the rear, the more power the rear side generates
photovoltaics-034.explanation: The rear side mainly receives light reflected from the ground and diffuse light from the sky. The more reflective the ground, as with white sand or snow compared with grass, and the higher the mounting, which shrinks the shadow and lets reflected light reach the rear, the more the rear side generates. Under some conditions the gain over a monofacial module exceeds 10%, and the rear contribution varies widely with installation. A higher cell temperature lowers the open-circuit voltage and efficiency on both sides, so a larger rear contribution in summer is wrong. A nearly constant gain overlooks the effects of ground reflectance and height.

photovoltaics-035.question: In electroluminescence (EL) inspection, a forward current is passed through a solar module in the dark and the light emitted by the cells is photographed, revealing cracks and broken contacts. Which describes the method correctly?
choices: The cells emit visible green light under forward current, so an ordinary camera can locate the defects from local differences in brightness
Injected carriers recombine radiatively and silicon emits near-infrared light at about 1150 nm; cracked areas without current and areas with heavy recombination appear dark
Current crowds into the narrowed paths at cracks and makes them glow brighter than their surroundings, so the brightest spots in a near-infrared image mark the cracks
photovoltaics-035.explanation: When forward current injects electrons and holes into the junction, some recombine radiatively and emit light at about 1150 nm, near the silicon band gap. Because silicon is an indirect semiconductor the emission is weak, but cooled silicon or InGaAs cameras can capture it. Regions disconnected from the contacts by cracks or broken fingers carry no current and stay dark, and defective regions with heavy recombination are dark too. The brightness reflects the local carrier density, so the method also maps cell quality. No visible green light is emitted, so ordinary photography shows nothing. Bright glowing cracks reverse the actual contrast.
